reading.body:
Forbes Tate's AI lobbying practice is concentrated: two clients, CoreWeave and Universal Music Group, account for 28 of the 42 AI filings, and one lobbyist, Franklyn Steinberg, appears on 30.

The client list is the pattern worth noting. CoreWeave is a GPU cloud provider, the kind of company whose business depends on data center capacity and power contracts. Universal Music Group is a rights holder whose AI exposure runs through training data and licensing. Imagine Learning is education software. Honda is a manufacturer. These are not AI developers lobbying on model policy. They are customers and suppliers of AI infrastructure and content, which means the filings likely track procurement, deployment, and liability questions rather than frontier research rules.

The lobbyist counts show how the work is staffed. Steinberg at 30 filings, Rachel Miller at 26, Cynthia Brown at 23, and four more names in the low twenties suggest a small core team carrying most of the portfolio, with a long tail of single-filing names. That is a generalist government affairs shop, not a specialist AI practice.

What the data does not say is what any of these clients argued. A filing reports that a firm lobbied on an issue, not the position taken, and the only bill named here is S 2714. The counts measure activity, not influence, and they cover only this firm's disclosures.
